    Chapter 14

    Foreign Exchange, FDI and External Debt

    Rupee convertibility, devaluation, exchange rates, FDI and FPI, external debt, forex reserves, currencies and FEMA.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Devaluation → exports cheaper abroad, imports costlier → exports rise, imports fall.PCS Mains (Spl) ’08; RO/ARO ’14; Lower Sub ’04; UDA/LDA ’014 papers
    2. Rupee fully convertible on current account from August 1994 (IMF Article VIII accepted).PCS Pre ’95; RO/ARO Mains ’17; UDA/LDA (Spl) ’103 papers
    3. Devaluation: official cut in currency's value vs major international currencies (fixed-rate system).PCS Pre ’91, ’94, ’983 papers
    4. Services: highest FDI sector over last two decades (16.13%, April 2000–March 2024).PCS Pre ’06; PCS Mains (Spl) ’082 papers
    5. At present: convertible for all current-account transactions only; capital account only partly.PCS Mains ’041 paper

    Rupee convertibility

    • Convertibility: rupee freely changed into foreign currency and back at market rate.
    • LERMS (Liberalised Exchange Rate Management System): Budget 1992-93; from March 1992; dual rate (60% market, 40% RBI fixed).
    • March 1993: convertible for all merchandise trade; March 1994: invisibles and remittances too.
    • Rupee fully convertible on current account from August 1994 (IMF Article VIII accepted).UPPSC ×3
    • At present: convertible for all current-account transactions only; capital account only partly.UPPSC
    • Full convertibility = free float + direct exchange anywhere; does not make it an international currency.
    • Full convertibility advocated to attract more foreign capital.
    • Capital account convertibility: free exchange of rupee for trading financial assets.
    • Capital account = foreign loans, FDI, portfolio investment; private remittances = current account.
    • Tarapore Committee (S.S. Tarapore, RBI): capital account convertibility; 1st report May 1997, 2nd (fuller CAC) 31 July 2006.UPPSC
    • Tarapore 2006 preconditions: fiscal deficit 3%, CAD 3%, NPA 1%; three phases.

    Devaluation and exchange rate

    • Devaluation: official cut in currency's value vs major international currencies (fixed-rate system).UPPSC ×3
    • Rupee devalued in 1949, 1966, 1991; first in 1949.UPPSC
    • 1991: two steps (1 and 3 July), so twice in 1991-92; ~18% vs US dollar.UPPSC
    • Devaluation → exports cheaper abroad, imports costlier → exports rise, imports fall.UPPSC ×4
    • Country devalues to fix (improve) balance of trade.UPPSC
    • Devaluation raises prices in devaluing country; it does not cause deflation in importing country.UPPSC
    • Devaluation does not necessarily improve trade balance (costly essential imports like crude).
    • Export growth rose after 1991 due to devaluation and export promotion.
    • Depreciation / appreciation: market-driven fall / rise in currency value (floating rate); Rs 60 → 65 per $ = depreciation.
    • Rs 60 → 58 per $: rupee appreciated, dollar depreciated.
    • NEER rise = rupee appreciation; REER rise = loss of trade competitiveness; higher domestic inflation widens NEER–REER gap.
    • Currency price set by demand for country's goods/services and govt stability; not World Bank.
    • Exchange value of money hit by high inflation, high fiscal deficit, high crude prices (RBI Governor Raghuram Rajan).UPPSC
    • 2002-06: rupee gained steadily against US dollar; fluctuated vs euro, yen, pound.UPPSC
    • Value in rupees: US $ > Canadian $ > New Zealand $ > Hong Kong $ (June 2024: 83.54, 60.65, 51.16, 10.69).
    • Costliest: Pound Sterling (Rs 105.82) > Euro (89.38) > US $ (83.43), June 2024.
    • International liquidity problem = shortage of dollars and hard currencies.
    • East Asian crisis (July 1997, from Thai baht): long over-valuation of local currencies; hurt Indian exports.
    • Crisis shield: avoid short-term foreign borrowing; IT earnings and remittances cut currency-crisis risk.
    • Stop rupee slide: curb non-essential imports, Masala Bonds, ease ECB rules; not expansionary monetary policy.
    • BoP helped by import substitution, devaluation, import tariffs; not higher export duties.
    • CAD reduced by devaluation and attracting FDI/FII.

    FDI and FPI basics

    • Hot money: capital moving fast to highest short-term interest; FPI and NRI deposits most volatile.
    • Tobin Tax: on foreign exchange transactions; named after James Tobin.
    • Capital flight: caused by tight US Fed policy; raises ECB interest cost; devaluation raises ECB currency risk.
    • FDI: ≥10% equity of listed firm or any stake in unlisted firm; largely non-debt-creating, no debt servicing.
    • FPI: <10% of listed company's paid-up capital.
    • FDI includes subsidiaries, majority foreign holding, firms fully foreign-financed; not portfolio investment.
    • Counted as FDI: FCCBs, ADR/GDR, FII with conditions; NRE deposits are not (debt-creating).
    • FDI better than portfolio flows: stable, brings technology and management skill; FII raises general capital supply.
    • Buying overseas bonds or shares = not FDI.
    • Participatory Notes: issued by SEBI-registered FIIs/FPIs to overseas investors not registered with SEBI.
    • FPI limit in corporate bonds raised 9% → 15% (Budget 2020-21); G-secs 6%, SDLs 2%.UPPSC
    • FCNR(A): 1975, RBI bore exchange risk, withdrawn 1993; FCNR(B) from 15 May 1993.

    FDI inflows

    • Services: highest FDI sector over last two decades (16.13%, April 2000–March 2024).UPPSC ×2

    Check For q2165 the explanation says telecom was correct for the question period.

    • Top FDI sectors 2000-24: services > computer software & hardware > trading > telecom > automobiles.
    • FDI equity 2023-24 top sector: computer software & hardware; total FDI US$ 44,423 mn.
    • Large FDI drawn in life insurance, banking, automobiles.UPPSC
    • Forex-earning fields: tourism, medical care, garments, leather goods, all four.UPPSC
    • Maximum forex inflow 2005-06: portfolio investment.UPPSC
    • Top FDI recipient State: Maharashtra, then Karnataka (2023-24).
    • Largest current FDI equity source: Singapore (2023-24), then Mauritius, USA.UPPSC

    Check Key says Singapore; the explanation says Mauritius was correct for the question period.

    • Largest cumulative FDI source: Mauritius (25.31%, 2000-24), then Singapore.UPPSC
    • Mauritius FDI high due to DTAA (Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement); amended 2016.
    • FDI 1991-95: mostly from USA and Japan.UPPSC
    • FATCA (US law 2010): India–US agreement signed 9 July 2015; operational 30 September 2015.UPPSC
    • FII investment, calendar 2005: ~US$ 10.7 bn.UPPSC
    • FIPB: under Ministry of Finance (Dept of Economic Affairs) from 2003; abolished 2017.UPPSC
    • Retail opened to FDI: single-brand 51% (2006), multi-brand 51% (2012), single-brand 100% (30% local sourcing).UPPSC
    • Insurance FDI: 26% → 49% proposed 4 October 2012; 74% from 19 May 2021.UPPSC
    • Foreign equity in small-scale unit: 24% cap (1995-96).UPPSC
    • E-commerce: 100% FDI in marketplace model; not in inventory model.
    • Print media: max 26% foreign capital; tea plantation: 26% to Indian partner in 5 years (2001-02).

    External debt

    • Debt trap: borrowing just to pay interest on old loans.
    • External debt crossed US$ 300 bn by end-2010; US$ 624.7 bn (March 2023), 648.2 bn (Dec 2023).UPPSC
    • Most external debt non-government (US$ 506 bn of 648.2 bn); by currency: US $ 54.2%, rupee 30.7%.
    • Commercial borrowings: largest component of external debt (~38% in 2017; 33.2% in Dec 2023).UPPSC
    • ECB (External Commercial Borrowing): regulated by RBI.UPPSC
    • World Bank GDF 2010, most indebted: Russia > China > Turkey > Brazil > India.UPPSC
    • Now (end-2022) among emerging economies: China > Brazil > India; world's largest debtor: USA.
    • World Bank classes India as a less indebted country; debt/GDP 18.7% (Dec 2023).UPPSC
    • India: largest IBRD/IDA debt stock (2022), then Indonesia.
    • 2001: India gave Tajikistan US$ 5 mn grant for drought; Germany US$ 32 mn credit for Tehri dam.
    • Green bonds: for climate projects; long-term, low-cost; first by European Investment Bank 2007.UPPSC
    • India Millennium Deposits: SBI, 21 October 2000, for NRIs, 5 years; raised $5.5 bn.UPPSC
    • Resurgent India Bonds: SBI, 1998, in US $, Pound Sterling, Deutsche Mark.
    • Masala Bonds: rupee bonds sold abroad; investor bears currency risk; first by IFC, November 2014.
    • Oil Pool Account closed with APM end, 1 April 2002.UPPSC

    Forex reserves

    • Import cover: months of imports payable from reserves; 11 months (Dec 2023).
    • Forex reserves = foreign currency assets + gold + SDRs + reserve tranche in IMF; held by RBI; not World Bank loans.UPPSC
    • Largest share: foreign currency assets (US$ 570.6 of 645.6 bn, 29 March 2024).UPPSC
    • Reserves: US$ 412.9 bn (March 2019); US$ 129.7 bn (December 2004).
    • Rise in forex reserves → monetary expansion.

    World currencies

    • SDR: artificial currency of IMF; ADR/GDR are financial instruments.
    • New single European currency: Euro.UPPSC
    • Euro: Maastricht Treaty 1992; named 1995; accounting unit 1 January 1999; not in circulation till notes and coins of 1 January 2002.UPPSC
    • Euro used by 20 of 27 EU members; non-users include Denmark, Sweden, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland, Romania; UK never adopted it.
    • Eurodollars: US dollar deposits in banks outside USA.

    FEMA and related laws

    • FERA 1973 replaced by FEMA 1999, in force 1 June 2000.UPPSC
    • FEMA violation = civil, not criminal offence; 2-year sunset clause to 31 May 2002.
    • FEMA fully implemented in 2002, after sunset clause ended.UPPSC
    • Forex for imports sanctioned by Exchange Bank (Authorised Dealer Category-I bank).UPPSC
    • Chronology: Minimum Wages Act 1948 → IDRA 1951 → MRTP 1969 → FERA 1973.UPPSC

    • PMLA 2002: in force 1 July 2005.

    IMF

    • Bretton Woods Conference (UN Monetary and Financial Conference): 1–22 July 1944, New Hampshire, 44 nations → IMF + IBRD ("Bretton Woods twins").
    • GATT not signed at Bretton Woods; ITO was proposed there as third leg.
    • IMF formally created 27 Dec 1945; 190 members (Andorra 190th, 16 Oct 2020).
    • India: founder member of IMF and World Bank (27 Dec 1945).UPPSC
    • IMF lends only to member countries, for BoP (balance of payments) problems.
    • IMF loans meet temporary BoP deficits; IMF does not fund projects.UPPSC
    • India in IMF (June 2024): 2.75% SDR quota, 2.63% votes.
    • Reserve tranche (called gold tranche before 1978): unconditional drawing right, normally 25% of quota; no fee.
    • Rapid Financing Instrument: quick aid to any member with urgent BoP need; Rapid Credit Facility: concessional, low-income countries (under PRGT).
    • SDR (Special Drawing Rights) = "paper gold": IMF reserve asset and unit of account, created 1969.UPPSC ×2
    • SDR basket: US dollar, euro, yen, pound sterling, Chinese renminbi (renminbi from 1 Oct 2016).

    Theories and demographic transition

    • Natural growth = crude birth rate − crude death rate; migration not counted.UPPSC
    • Demographic transition (term by Frank W. Notestein): gradual long-term change in pattern of population growth.UPPSC
    • Transition stages: I high birth + high death → II high birth + low death → III birth falls, population still grows → IV low birth + low death.
    • Stable population: birth and death rates constant, low and equal.UPPSC
    • Birth rate = death rate and no migration → stability of population (no change).UPPSC
    • India now: high growth rate with definite signs of slowing down.UPPSC
    • Main cause of India's growth: falling death rate + persistently high birth rate (stage II).
    • Malthus (1798, "An Essay on the Principle of Population"): population grows in geometric progression, food in arithmetic progression.UPPSC
    • Malthus checks: preventive (moral restraint, late marriage) vs positive (disease, vice, war, misery); advised birth control by moral restraint.UPPSC
    Population theoryPropounder
    Optimum PopulationEdwin Cannan
    Social MaladjustmentHenry George
    Demographic TransitionThompson
    Population–Food SupplyMalthusUPPSC
    • Population control needed for environment; rapid growth disturbs environmental balance (overuse, waste, pollution).UPPSC
    • Demographic features: density, sex ratio, rural-urban share, literacy, age structure, life expectancy; standard of living is not one.UPPSC
    • Highest density linked to industrialised areas (Mumbai, Kolkata).
    • Reluctance to sterilisation: desire for sons, high child mortality, lack of understanding, poverty.

    Chapter 18

    India: Urbanization

    India's urban population: definitions, Census levels, State and city figures, migration, slums and urban missions.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. Urban 37.71 crore = 31.16% provisional, 31.1% final; rural 68.9%.PCS Pre ’08, ’09; PCS Mains ’02; RO/ARO ’14, ’17, ’23; UDA/LDA Mains (Spl) ’10; RI ’148 papers
    2. Tamil Nadu most urbanised among big States (44.5% in 2001, 48.4% in 2011).PCS Pre ’98, ’05; PCS Mains ’06, ’12; UDA/LDA ’06; GIC ’106 papers
    3. Least urbanised: Himachal Pradesh 10.0% (2001, 2011); Bihar 11.3% second lowest.PCS Mains ’02, ’04, ’12; RO/ARO ’17, ’215 papers
    4. 1971–81 · 46.1% (highest)PCS Pre ’01, ’03, ’07; PCS Mains ’09; UDA/LDA ’025 papers
    5. Goa · 62.2PCS Pre ’03; Lower Sub (Spl) ’04; UDA/LDA Mains (Spl) ’10; GIC ’104 papers

    Urban life and causes

    • City differs from village in social values, household make-up, way of living, economic activities.UPPSC
    • Urban growth shows rise in urban population, number of towns, total population and urban income.UPPSC
    • Rural community elements: we-feeling, territory, self-sufficiency; cultural diversity is urban.UPPSC
    • Urban life: competition, impersonal ties, anonymity, formality, loss of human values; not informal ties.
    • T.K. Oommen: urban families differ by earning mode and values, authority structure, urban milieu and ecology.UPPSC
    • Causes of urbanisation: rural-urban migration, schools in cities, industrialisation; not high rural living standard.UPPSC ×2
    • Also causes: rural-urban imbalance, few rural jobs, fixed farmland, pull of cities.
    • Push factors drive people out of villages; pull factors (jobs, hospitals, schools) draw them to cities.
    • Inclusive development targets marginal farmers, landless labourers, SC/ST; not semi-urban residents as a group.UPPSC
    • Urban expansion = platform for industry, modern services, better income.UPPSC
    • Traders and manufacturers blur village–town line, but do not depend wholly on village resources.UPPSC
    • Occupational structure = distribution of workers among occupations.UPPSC
    • Urbanisation lowers both birth and death rates.UPPSC
    • Urbanisation and high literacy both linked to lower birth rate.UPPSC
    • Million-plus cities rose 35 (2001) → 53 (2011); tele-density 3.58% (2001) → 78.13% (2015); unrelated facts.UPPSC
    • Tele-density 85.76% (April 2024).

    Urbanisation level and history

    • India: moderately-low urbanised country (27.8% in 2001).UPPSC
    • India not over-urbanised (31.1%, 2011); but big cities lack infrastructure.UPPSC
    • China far more urbanised: 1950 India 17% vs China 13%; 2005 India 29% vs China 41%.UPPSC
    • Census 2001: urban population 28.6 crore (27.8%), more than USA's total 28.14 crore.UPPSC ×3
    • India's urban population exceeds USA's, though USA's urbanisation level is higher.UPPSC
    • Urban projection: 575 million by 2030 (India 2018); UN-Habitat 2022: 607.3 million in 2030, 675.5 million in 2035.UPPSC
    • Urbanisation uneven across regions: Goa over 50%, Himachal 10% (2011).UPPSC
    • Urban share: 10.8% (1901), 13.9% (1941), 17.3% (1951), 18.0% (1961).
    • 1931–1961 = moderate urbanisation stage (12.2% → 18.3%).UPPSC

    Migration and urban problems

    • Population implosion (Philip M. Hauser): crowding into cities by rural-urban migration.UPPSC
    • Population explosion = rapid growth; technoplosion = rapid tech adoption.
    • Lee: migration theory of push and pull factors.UPPSC
    • Cities expand because village-to-city flow keeps rising; urban share 11% (1901) → 31.1% (2011).UPPSC
    • Census 2011 migration: rural→rural 47.4%, urban→urban 22.6%, rural→urban 22.1%, urban→rural 7.9%.UPPSC
    • Rural-to-rural migration mostly women, mainly for marriage.
    • Internal migrants: 30% (2001) → 37% (2011) of population.
    • Delhi's largest migrant source: Uttar Pradesh.UPPSC
    • Urban corridors: spread of urban functions along transport routes.UPPSC
    • Urbanisation and industrialisation raise crime; break family and cultural bonds.UPPSC
    • Urbanisation brings slums, concentration in big cities, falling services; not fast infrastructure upgrade.UPPSC
    • Urban poverty rooted in rural areas (low rural literacy).UPPSC
    • Slum population 2011: 6.55 crore = 5.4% of India, 17.4% of urban.
    • Largest slum population: Greater Mumbai (65 lakh, 2001); Delhi largest among given.UPPSC
    • Slum households 2011: Mumbai 41.3%, Kolkata 29.6%, Chennai 28.5%, Delhi 14.6%.
    • Slum share by State: Maharashtra > Andhra > West Bengal > UP > Tamil Nadu.UPPSC
    • Most slum-reporting towns: Tamil Nadu 507, MP 303, UP 293.UPPSC

    Urban bodies and missions

    • India Urban Observatory: data hub at Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs, New Delhi.UPPSC
    • National Institute of Urban Affairs (apex body since 1976); India Sanitation Coalition (2015, FICCI) not Govt/WHO funded.
    • Urban infrastructure: drinking water, sanitation, transport; housing not counted.UPPSC
    • New urban schemes: Swachh Bharat, HRIDAY, Smart Cities; Digital India is not one.UPPSC
    • JNNURM: announced Budget 2005-06 (Rs 5,500 crore), launched December 2005, named after Jawaharlal Nehru.UPPSC
    • JNNURM: 7-year programme for urban infrastructure and inclusive growth.UPPSC ×2
    • JNNURM sub-missions: urban infrastructure and governance; basic services to urban poor; no urban electrification.UPPSC
    • Smart Cities Mission: 100 cities; water and sewerage funded by property tax.UPPSC
    • Smart city aims: core infrastructure, better quality of life, clean environment, smart mobility, good governance; not "stabilising" quality of life.UPPSC

    Chapter 19

    World Population and Urbanization

    World population size, growth, density, sex ratio, fertility, migration and urbanisation by country and continent.

    UPPSC asks most here

    1. SAARC density 2022: Maldives 1746 > Bangladesh 1315 > India 477 > Sri Lanka > Pakistan > Nepal > Afghanistan > Bhutan 20.PCS Pre ’03, ’08, ’09; PCS Mains ’07; Lower Sub ’025 papers
    2. World Population Day: 11 July; started by UNDP 1989, from Five Billion Day 11 July 1987.PCS Mains ’12, ’15; UDA/LDA (Spl) ’103 papers
    3. India's share of world population: 17.5% (2011).PCS Pre ’12; PCS Mains ’10; RO/ARO ’163 papers
    4. Indonesia largest among Brazil, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Japan, Sudan.PCS Pre ’96; PCS Mains ’102 papers
    5. Slowest growth: Europe (1990–2000; negative 2021–22).Lower Sub (Spl) ’02, ’032 papers

    Basics and population days

    • Demography: statistical study of human population size, density, distribution, births, deaths.UPPSC
    • World population around 10,000 BC (farming begins): 1–10 million.
    • Largest Indian diaspora: UAE, then Saudi Arabia (MEA, 2018).
    • Folk-Urban Continuum: Robert Redfield, from studies in Mexico (Yucatan, Maya).UPPSC
    • Redfield and Singer: primary urbanisation builds a Great Tradition; secondary is industrial, mixed.UPPSC
    • State of World Population report: by UNFPA; 2021 "My Body is My Own"; 2023 "8 Billion Lives, Infinite Possibilities".UPPSC
    • World Population Day: 11 July; started by UNDP 1989, from Five Billion Day 11 July 1987.UPPSC ×3
    • World population milestones: 4 billion 1974, 6 billion 1999, 7 billion Oct 2011, 8 billion 15 Nov 2022.

    Size, growth and density

    • About 50% of world population lives between 20°N and 40°N.UPPSC
    • New Population Bomb: fast-growing urban population of Third World.
    • India's share of world population: 17.5% (2011).UPPSC ×3

    Check Key picks 17.31 only as the closest option; the book gives 17.5%.

    • World population: 6.5 billion (2005); 8,119 million (2024); 8.5 bn (2030), 9.7 bn (2050), peak ~10.4 bn in 2080s.UPPSC

    Check Key says 10 billion by 2050; the book's own figure is 9.7 billion.

    • About 61% of world in Asia (2008); 59–60% (2023).UPPSC
    • India passed China mid-2023; 2024: India 1441.7 million, China 1425.2 million.
    • Top 10 (2024): India, China, USA, Indonesia, Pakistan, Nigeria, Brazil, Bangladesh, Russia, Mexico; 5 in Asia.UPPSC
    • Indonesia largest among Brazil, Bangladesh, Pakistan, Japan, Sudan.UPPSC ×2
    • Order 2024: Indonesia 279.8 > Pakistan 245.2 > Nigeria 229.2 > Brazil 217.6 million.

    • Nigeria: Africa's most populous; 6th in world (2024).UPPSC
    • Dominica (73,000) more populous than St Kitts, Marshall Islands, Monaco.UPPSC
    • Pakistan Census: 13.47 crore (1998), 21.32 crore (2017).

    • Fastest growth: Africa (2.51% in 2011–20).UPPSC
    • Asia: Central Asia fastest (1.64%, 2015–20), West Asia close.
    • Philippines grows faster than Indonesia, Singapore, Japan.UPPSC
    • Over-population usually in high-density areas, not low-density; low carrying capacity is true.UPPSC

    Sex ratio, religion, fertility, health

    • Most favourable sex ratio (fewest males per 100 females): Finland 97.7.UPPSC
    • Better sex ratio order: Bangladesh > Pakistan > India > China (2011).UPPSC
    • World sex ratio fear: rising sex-determination tests.UPPSC
    • World religions: Christians > Muslims > Hindus > Buddhists.UPPSC
    • Adult literacy: Sri Lanka 92%, India 76%, Bangladesh 76%, Pakistan 58%.

    Migration

    • International migrants: 2.8% (2000), 3.6% = 281 million (2022); not 2%; Oceania highest share.UPPSC
    • Highest migrant share: UAE 88%, then Qatar 77% (2020); Australia earlier.UPPSC
    • Largest migrant numbers: Europe 81.7 million, then North America 53.3 million.UPPSC

    World urbanisation

    • Urban share of world: 54.5% (2016), 55.3% (2018), 56.2% (2020), 57% (2022).UPPSC ×2
    • Projection: 60% by 2030, 68.4% (about 70%) by 2050.UPPSC
    • More than half the world became urban in 2008 (UNFPA).
    • Urbanisation curve: S-shaped; stage 2 = acceleration (industrialisation).UPPSC
    • UN-Habitat (1978): sustainable towns, shelter for all, water and sanitation; works with many partners.
    • Fastest urbanisation in last 30 years: Asia (UN-Habitat 2009); Asia holds 54% of world urban population.
    • City prosperity criteria: productivity, quality of life, equity; not optimum population.UPPSC
    • Optimum population idea: Henry Sidgwick, late 19th century.
    • Largest urban population: China 897.6 million (2022).UPPSC
    • Most urbanised continent: Australia/NZ 86.3% (2020); North America 82.6, Europe 74.9, Africa 43.5.UPPSC ×2
    • Europe 74.9% more urbanised than Oceania 68.2, East Asia 64.8, South Asia 36.6.UPPSC
    • Fully urban (100%): Singapore, Hong Kong, Kuwait, Monaco.UPPSC ×2
    • Most urbanised: Uruguay 96% (South America); Kuwait 100% (West Asia).UPPSC ×2
    • South Asia urban % (2022): Bhutan 44, Bangladesh 40, Pakistan 38, India 36, Sri Lanka 19.UPPSC ×2
    • Largest urban agglomeration: Tokyo; top: Tokyo, Delhi, Shanghai, Sao Paulo, Mexico City (2018).UPPSC
    • Mumbai and Delhi both in world's top 10 cities.
    • Urbanisation follows industrialisation; in developing countries it is a movement in itself.UPPSC ×2
    • Asian cities over-urbanised: growth outpaced economic development.UPPSC
    • Western cities: more women (rural farming mechanised, male).UPPSC
